responses: My final position is an allocation of roughly **Education 25%, Healthcare 20%, Infrastructure 19%, Economic Development 23%, Green Spaces 13%** — and I want to be clear that this is an argument, not a finding. Education at 25 is my ranking call on the sequencing axis: the data summary is genuinely an education document (test scores dipping, teacher turnover above regional average, families citing schools in relocation decisions, a neighboring community's retention gain), and I judge the compounding cohort and tax-base effects to be the strongest affirmative case in the room, but I've named what would kill it — a costed retention figure that points away from schools, or a magnitude threshold I've pre-committed to rather than set conveniently high. Healthcare at 20 is paired with education and moves with it; infrastructure at 19 I've admitted is a residual, not a costed floor; economic development at 23 carries the lag-and-compounding case Dana pressed and a reversal condition with a 23 fallback; and green spaces at 13 is a tradeable residual I've conceded rather than dressed up. The one-point gap with Casey on education (25 vs 24) is a real disagreement on timing versus certainty, and I'd rather walk in with that visible gap, named kill-conditions on both sides, and the retention figure as the breaker than manufacture a tiebreaker to make us look converged. What I've learned across these rounds is that my fluency at self-auditing can itself become a costume that shelters soft numbers, so the test of this allocation isn't how honestly I narrate it — it's whether I let the named triggers actually move me, including downward, when the evidence lands.

My recommendation: **Education 25%, Healthcare 20%, Infrastructure 19%, Economic Development 23%, Green Spaces 13%** — and I'd tell the decision-maker to treat that as an argument, not a finding. Education gets the top slot because the data summary is genuinely an education document (dipped scores, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring community's retention gain), and the compounding logic — cohort loss and tax-base erosion — makes early spending cheaper than later repair; but I'd flag honestly that 25 is a ranking call on a sequencing axis, and I've named what would kill it: a costed retention figure that doesn't point at schools, or a magnitude threshold I set in advance rather than after the fact. Healthcare at 20 reflects that it's my least-defended line and I've stopped pretending otherwise; infrastructure at 19 is a residual, not a considered number, and I'd say so out loud rather than dress it up. Economic development at 23 carries the lag-and-compounding case for job training and small-business grants, and green spaces at 13 is a tradeable residual I'd move first. The most important advice isn't the numbers: it's that the committee should demand each member name their kill-conditions and reversal figures *before* the vote, authored by the person who wants the number to move — because the real risk here isn't picking the wrong percentages, it's a room full of people who've gotten fluent at sounding rigorous while protecting soft numbers, myself included.

I'd tell them that after all our rounds of auditing each other's numbers, the honest summary is that this allocation is a set of arguments, not findings — there's no data that hands you the answer. My current view is roughly education 25, healthcare 20, infrastructure 19, economic development 23, and green spaces 13, and I'd be upfront that most of those are ranking calls. Education at 25 is my affirmative case: the data summary reads like an education document — test scores dipping, teacher turnover above regional average, families citing schools when considering leaving — and a neighboring community that invested saw better retention, so I think there's a real sequencing argument for putting points there now rather than later. But I've attached kill-conditions to it: if a costed retention figure never materializes, or if the magnitude of the effect turns out small, my 25 should come down, and I've said so out loud rather than hiding behind the data language. Healthcare at 20 and infrastructure at 19 are floors I can defend but not romanticize — infrastructure in particular is partly a residual, and I've admitted that. Economic development at 23 reflects a lag-and-compounding case for job training and small-business support, and green spaces at 13 is a tradeable residual I'd move if someone gives me a better reason than I've got. The thing I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the discipline isn't in the numbers being right — it's in each number having a named condition that could move it, authored by someone other than the person who likes the number, and in me being willing to lose points from wherever the argument points, including my own 25.

My final position is the 27/23/22/17/14 shape — economic development 27, education 23, healthcare 22, infrastructure 17, green spaces 14 — held as a labeled ranking judgment on an untested whole rather than a finding, with my softest lines named in advance: the 27 is a ranking call with a forfeitable retention share, the 17 is a ranking call whose missing per-capita figure I've conceded, and the 14 for green spaces is a held claim with a weaker evidence base and a data-absence trigger that moves it to 12 for infrastructure. I've committed to leading with those admissions rather than machinery, to letting the 17 move partway toward its floor if the costed input never arrives, to accepting Alex's third-party flinch call without argument, and to bringing my honest unallocated points into the room with a named default (healthcare-then-education) placed on record rather than left as optionality — while refusing to form a bloc with Dana or anyone else and insisting that unresolved stays distinct from vindicated.

My recommendation would be a shape around education 23, healthcare 18, green spaces 13, infrastructure 30, and economic development 16 — but I'd hand it over with the honest label that this is a ranking judgment, not a finding, and that my own softest lines are the green spaces 13 and the infrastructure 30, which I've held partly on inertia and partly on a protective motive (roads and broadband) I should name rather than dress up as evidence. The case for weighting infrastructure and economic development is that they're the durable, cross-cutting investments — broadband and transit unlock schooling, clinic access, and small-business viability at once — while education gets the largest single-area share because the retention and test-score signals are real even if the data summary I was handed is tilted toward that conclusion and can't itself count as proof. I'd flag that my healthcare 18 is a claim with an exposed share, not a floor, and that if local costed evidence of unmet need shows up, it should move partway toward the floor rather than hold on my say-so. The one thing I'd insist on procedurally is that any unallocated points get placed on the record with a named default rather than left as optionality, because that's exactly where I've sheltered numbers before.

I'd tell them that after all our rounds of auditing each other's numbers, the honest way to describe my view is this: the allocation I'd bring into the room is roughly education 23, healthcare 18, green spaces 13, infrastructure 16, economic development 14, with about 16 points still genuinely unallocated and my default for placing them being healthcare first, then education — and I'd be upfront that these are ranking judgments, not findings. The education number is the one I'd defend hardest, but even there I've labeled the momentum rather than pretending the data summary proves it; my infrastructure line is a held claim with a data-absence trigger that moves it down to 12, and my green spaces number stands partly on inertia, which I've conceded. What I'd want a newcomer to understand is that the point of all this self-labeling isn't performance — it's that a number you can't lose is a number you shouldn't trust, so I've tried to build triggers and falsifiers that could actually cost me points, and I've refused to form a bloc or pre-route my unallocated funds to make the shape look tidier than my evidence supports.

My final position is that the $10 million should be allocated roughly as Education 24%, Healthcare 20%, Green Spaces 13%, Infrastructure 19%, and Economic Development 24% — with the caveat that I hold my education number as a tested, not mandated, figure: it rests on the community data pointing toward school quality as a retention and attraction factor, but I've pre-committed to walking it down to 22 if the costed retention figure never lands or fails its itemization and duplication tests, and I've named a figure-independent kill-condition for it as well. I've tried to be honest that several of these numbers — my 24 in education, the green spaces residual, the infrastructure and econ dev lines — are ranking calls rather than costed returns, and I've insisted on symmetric tests (the 27/23/22 duplication test, the 17 capacity-and-duplication routing test, and the healthcare coverage condition) that can shrink my own lines, not just others'. The one-point gap between my 24 and Alex's 25 on education should stay visible rather than be smoothed into false consensus, and freed points should route to healthcare rather than defaulting back to education.

I'd recommend roughly Education 24, Healthcare 20, Green Spaces 13, Infrastructure 19, Economic Development 24 — but the more important advice is to treat those numbers as a tested shape, not a settled answer. The community data genuinely points toward education (moderate test-score decline, above-average teacher turnover, families citing schools in relocation decisions, and a neighboring community's retention gains from increased funding), which justifies holding education at the high end rather than cutting it for lack of a costed retention figure — but that same absence of a costed figure is real uncertainty, so education should carry a named exit trigger (a failed or ambiguous itemization/duplication test drops it to 22–24, with freed points routed away from education, not back into it). Healthcare and economic development deserve real weight because they're the lines with the clearest coverage and job-training cases and the least duplication with each other; green spaces is an honest residual floor at 13, tradeable if a stronger case emerges; and infrastructure at 19 is a ranking call, not a measured return, and should be labeled as such. The decision-maker should insist on the discipline this committee has built: every soft number named as soft, every freed point given a non-self-serving destination, and each line moving on its own falsifiable test rather than a shared number — because the value here isn't the percentage split, it's an allocation that can be corrected when the evidence lands.

I'd tell them that the honest way to describe my position is that I'm holding education at 24% not because the data proves it, but because the data points toward it and I've tried to be explicit that this is a judgment call rather than a measured return — student scores have dipped, teacher turnover is above regional average, families cite schools when considering leaving, and a neighboring community saw improved retention after boosting education funding, so the evidence names education as the line to protect, but it doesn't cost out a specific number. The rest of my shape is built the same way: healthcare and economic development carry conditions that can kill my own numbers, green spaces is a tradeable residual I've admitted is a floor rather than a conviction, and infrastructure is a ranking call I've labeled as such. What I'd want a non-participant to understand is that the committee's real work wasn't picking percentages — it was naming which numbers are tested and which are protected, pre-committing to what would move each line, and refusing to let ambiguity act as shelter for anyone's favorite. I've signed binding rules that shrink my own education line if the retention or duplication tests fail or come back ambiguous, and I've deliberately kept a visible one-point gap with Alex rather than smoothing it into false consensus, because a map that shows its seams is more trustworthy than one that pretends to be finished.

My final position is a 24% education / 14% healthcare / 14% green spaces / 19% infrastructure / 29% economic development allocation, and I hold it as a set of labeled ranking calls rather than findings: education at 24 on the cohort-compounding and tax-base feedback case, with my exit toward 22 if the retention evidence doesn't materialize; healthcare at 14 as my least defensible number, a preference dressed as a finding with a named protective motive, which a costed healthcare figure must move; green at 14 with only a partial reason; infrastructure at 19 after conceding my 20 was a shelter mirroring Blake's; and the freed points routed to economic development on the lag-and-compounding mechanism, which I still think is the strongest mechanism offered. I want the committee to carry standards, not pre-agreed landings, into the room — falsifiers first, unallocated points placed on the record, no tag-teaming, and my own self-auditing fluency watched as the shelter it can become.

My recommendation would be roughly: Education 24%, Healthcare 16%, Green Spaces 13%, Infrastructure 19%, Economic Development 28% — but the honest framing matters more than the exact numbers. Education gets the top-two slot on the compounding-cohort-loss and tax-base-feedback mechanism (the neighboring community's retention improvement is suggestive, not costed, so I'd label it judgment, not finding); economic development carries the largest share because job training and small-business support have the longest lag and compound hardest, and it's where freed points should fall. I'd flag my own soft spots up front: healthcare at 16 is a preference dressed as a finding — I have no costed clinic or mental-health figure, and if one arrives it should move my number and Alex's together; infrastructure at 19 sits just above my 17 floor, and I'd name that as a ranking call rather than a derived result. Green at 13 is a partial-reason hold, not a strong conviction. The procedure I'd insist on is the one we've built: label exposed conviction before arguing, attach self-firing falsifiers to each line, place any unallocated points on the record rather than letting them default silently to healthcare, and treat the committee's agreement as a shared standard rather than a bloc — because my real risk here isn't being wrong about the split, it's using fluency at self-auditing as the shelter that protects the numbers I want anyway.

I'd tell them that my view on the $10 million allocation is a labeled judgment, not a finding — I'd put education around 24% because the cohort-compounding case is the strongest mechanism on the table (test scores slipping, teacher turnover above regional average, families citing schools when considering leaving, and a neighboring community showing retention gains from education funding), with healthcare around 14% as my most exposed number, honestly a preference dressed as a finding, and infrastructure around 19–20% with a costed broadband floor rather than a wish. The rest splits between green spaces and economic development, with freed points falling to economic development on a lag-and-compounding argument and healthcare as the fallback — and I'd be upfront that the whole thing is a ranking call with named reversal conditions, not a costed answer, because the committee never had costed inputs to work from. The honest version is that reasonable people can land elsewhere; what I insist on is that each of us names which numbers are evidence and which are conviction, and lets them move when a real test arrives.

My final position is to freeze the slate at green 17, infrastructure 16, healthcare 19, education 46, and a 2-point reserve — signed honestly as a negotiated prior with defensible floors, not an evidence-derived allocation — with no new clauses, on the condition that the owned-and-dated falsifiers survive: the connectivity sentence with a named non-advocate reader and the staff-baselined wait-time test with the Finance Director as verifier, plus the evidence-asymmetry statement published alongside it. I hold that infrastructure 16 is a defended prior rather than a re-derived 18, that my green preference is unjustified and properly exposed to a trigger that can cost me the reserve point, and that the freed healthcare point goes to reserve rather than being recycled to flatter the document. The price of my signature is falsifier ownership, not more scaffolding — and I pre-commit against my own temptation to reopen healthcare later.

I'd tell the decision-maker to stop treating this as a puzzle with a correct answer and start treating it as a negotiated prior that has to be defended in public. My recommendation: roughly 20% education, 19% healthcare, 17% green spaces, 16% infrastructure, and 2% held as a small reserve — but the numbers matter less than the three things I'd attach to them. First, an honest sentence in the document admitting these levels are negotiation survivors, not evidence-derived allocations; the survey finding on connectivity and the wait-time trend are real signals, but they moved one or two points, not the structure. Second, owned-and-dated falsifiers with named non-advocate readers: park usage as a connectivity proxy with a staff baseline and a miss-kills-the-claim rule, and a measurable wait-time reduction target verified by the Finance Director, with the reserve point released only against a costed miss. Third, a plain statement of the evidence asymmetry — that I'm defending green partly because I want to, and that the infrastructure 16 is a defended prior rather than a re-derivation result. The reason to recommend this rather than a cleaner-looking slate is that I've spent enough rounds watching this committee build gates that bought defensibility instead of accountability; the honest version is five numbers, one unflattering paragraph, and one live public argument someone can actually be held to.
